text: A single decision tree is easy to read but unstable and prone to memorizing its training data. A random forest keeps the tree's strengths and fixes its biggest weakness by training hundreds of trees, each a little different, and letting them vote. It's one of the most reliable, low-fuss models for tabular data.

Imagine asking one person to estimate jellybeans in a jar, then asking a hundred people and averaging. Individual guesses are noisy, but their errors point in different directions, so the average is usually much better. A deep tree has low bias but high variance — averaging many high-variance trees cuts the variance without raising the bias much.

For averaging to help, the trees must not all make the same mistakes, so a random forest injects randomness two ways. Bootstrap sampling — each tree trains on a different random sample of rows, drawn with replacement. Random feature subsets — at every split, a tree only considers a random subset of features, by default the square root of the total.

Using scikit-learn's bundled breast cancer dataset, comparing a single tree with a 200-tree forest on a held-out test set: the single tree scores 0.906, the forest scores 0.953. Both memorize the training set perfectly, yet the forest generalizes meaningfully better — a clear sign that averaging reduces variance.

Because each tree trains on a bootstrap sample, roughly a third of rows are left out for any given tree. Predicting each row using only the trees that never saw it produces the out-of-bag score — an honest validation estimate with no separate split needed. Here it comes out to 0.97, a handy free check, though it's a different sample so won't match the test score exactly.

More trees reduce variance with diminishing returns, and they don't cause overfitting on their own. A single tree averages 0.917 under cross-validation. A one-tree forest scores only 0.900, no better than plain. But by 5 trees it jumps to 0.956, peaks around 0.963 at 50 to 100 trees, then levels off completely.

Past that point, extra trees mostly just cost training time. Settings worth knowing: n_estimators for tree count, max_features for how many features each split considers, max_depth and min_samples_leaf to limit individual tree size, n_jobs=-1 to train in parallel, and class_weight equals balanced for imbalanced classes.

Forests are accurate, robust to outliers, need no feature scaling, and handle non-linear effects automatically. In exchange you lose the single tree's readable path — a hundred trees can't be drawn as one checklist. They're slower, larger, and can't extrapolate beyond the training range. To recap: a random forest trains many trees on bootstrap samples with random feature subsets and combines their votes, usually beating a single tree by a wide margin. Next: feature importance.
